title: Education Hart, Nick Grasping the Opportunity of the Inclusive Teaching Framework
author: Hart, Nick
summary: Ambition Institute's Inclusive Teaching Framework organizes specialist knowledge for educating students with SEND into five domains and translates it into classroom-accessible language for teachers rather than clinicians. Hart argues that the publication's value depends entirely on how school leaders choose to use it: the risk is treating it like any policy document (acknowledge, file, move on); the opportunity is using it in three specific ways: as a mirror to audit current practice honestly, as a focus lens guided by the inclusion register's most common barriers, and as a tool to bolster wave 1 teaching by weaving inclusive strategies into the existing pedagogical framework. Hart recommends going narrow and deep: one domain, one year group, one honest conversation about what is actually happening in classrooms.
points: * The quality of teaching is the most significant influence on outcomes for students with SEND -- making the Inclusive Teaching Framework's translation of specialist knowledge into classroom language a significant practical resource. * The three honest uses: as a mirror (auditing what actually happens in classrooms), as a focus lens (guided by the inclusion register's most common barriers), and as a tool for bolstering wave 1 teaching by embedding strategies rather than delegating them to specialists. * The temptation when a national framework lands is to respond at the highest level -- whole-school launch, new policy, CPD programme -- but the better move is often to go narrow and deep. * Most SEND knowledge in a school is held in a couple of people's heads without much deliberate upstream decision-making -- the framework's audit function reveals how much inclusive practice is actually informal and person-dependent. * Inclusive strategies should be woven into the existing pedagogical framework rather than siloed as a specialist add-on.
quotes: In the UK and the UAE, inclusion is a national priority, with both governments looking to set a standard for educating children with SEND to improve long term outcomes.
The quality of teaching is the most significant influence on outcomes for students and arguably even more so for students with SEND.

Read it. Actually read it, not just grab an AI summary. Then as leaders we decide what we do with it. The risk is that we treat it like any other policy document: acknowledge it, file it, and move on.
It's easy to nod along to the recommendations: visual cues? Yep. Scaffolding? We've been talking about it for years. Predictable environment? Of course. It's a start, but we can do better.
My guess is that a lot of this will be held in a couple of people's heads without too much deliberate, upstream decision making.
The Inclusive Teaching Framework is not designed to be handed to SENDCos, inclusion teachers or LSAs as a guide to intervene.

The temptation when a national framework lands is to respond at the highest level. But we might instead consider going narrow and deep: one domain, one year group, one honest conversation about what's actually happening in classrooms.
